steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our DiffSal paper, a diffusion model for audio-visual saliency prediction. Motivate the AVSP task, discuss the limits of existing approaches, introduce the method, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- AVSP task and applications
- Existing approaches: localization-based, 3D convolution-based
- Two challenges; diffusion models as an opportunity
- DiffSal: overview of training and inference
- Two properties of DiffSal
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- AVSP task
  - humans focus quickly on interesting areas using visual + auditory systems
  - visual attention in multi-modal scenarios -> audio-visual saliency prediction (AVSP)
  - applications: video summarization (cite), compression (cite), virtual reality (cite), augmented reality (cite)
- Existing approaches
  - efforts: better multimodal interaction, more generalizable model structures
  - localization-based methods (cite), Figure 1 (a): sounding objects as saliency targets; saliency -> spatial sound source localization; consider audio-visual semantic interaction but little focus on generalized network -> constrained performance
  - 3D convolution-based methods (cite), Figure 1 (b): superior performance but customized architectures, inductive biases for saliency
  - e.g. Jain et al. (cite) and Xiong et al. (cite): 3D encoder-decoder like UNet, empirical designs in the decoder
  - both families: sophisticated loss functions -> intricate modeling paradigm
- Challenges and diffusion
  - two factors for real-world AVSP: effective audio-visual interaction, generalized saliency network; not sufficiently exploited
  - diffusion models (cite): strong generalization; unified framework for generative tasks conditioned on class labels (cite), text prompts (cite), images (cite), sounds (cite)
  - open question: diffusion model meeting both requirements
- DiffSal, Figure 1 (c)
  - conditional Diffusion model for generalized audio-visual Saliency prediction
  - video + audio as conditions; saliency prediction as conditional generation of saliency map
  - training: video, audio, degraded saliency map (ground truth + varying noise)
  - two-stream encoder: audio/video feature pairs, spatio-temporal coherence; pixel-wise multi-modal features guide generation
  - Saliency-UNet recovers saliency maps from noisy inputs, conditioned on spatio-temporal audio/video features
  - multi-modal interaction mechanism for latent semantic associations
  - simple mean square error loss
  - inference: reversed diffusion, multi-step denoising from random noisy saliency maps
- Properties
  - (i) unlike methods with spatio-temporal visual branching (cite): spatio-temporal modeling of audio and video; audio-only, video-only, audio-visual
  - (ii) iterative denoising -> reuse Saliency-UNet to improve without retraining
- Contributions
  - (1) conditional generative formulation; conditional diffusion saliency model
  - (2) two properties: uni-/multi-modal; iterative refinement without retraining
  - (3) six audio-visual benchmarks; average relative improvement of 6.3% over previous SOTA across four metrics

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Humans have visual and auditory sensory systems, and with them they can quickly focus on the most interesting areas in their daily activities. This capability of visual attention in multi-modal scenarios has been studied by many researchers and it is called the audio-visual saliency prediction (AVSP) task. Based on the related techniques there are many useful practical applications, from video summarization and compression to virtual reality and augmented reality.

A lot of effort has gone into this area, focusing on improving the quality of multimodal interaction and making the model structures more generalizable. Among the common AVSP approaches, localization-based methods have gotten a lot of attention, as shown in Figure 1 (a). These methods usually treat the sounding objects in the scene as the saliency targets and turn the saliency prediction task into a spatial sound source localization problem. These methods do consider the semantic interactions between audio and visual modalities, but they still do not focus much on a generalized network structure, and this leads to constrained performance.

On the other hand, recent 3D convolution-based methods show better performance in predicting audio-visual saliency maps, as shown in Figure 1 (b). But these methods need customized architectures with built-in inductive biases that are tailored for saliency prediction tasks. For example, Jain et al. and Xiong et al. both use a 3D encoder-decoder structure similar to UNet, but they put their empirical designs into the decoder. Also, both the localization-based and the 3D convolution-based methods use sophisticated loss functions, which makes the audio-visual saliency modeling paradigm more intricate.

- Challenges and diffusion
  - two factors for real-world AVSP: effective audio-visual interaction, generalized saliency network; not sufficiently exploited
  - diffusion models (cite): strong generalization; unified framework for generative tasks conditioned on class labels (cite), text prompts (cite), images (cite), sounds (cite)
  - open question: diffusion model meeting both requirements
- DiffSal, Figure 1 (c)
  - conditional Diffusion model for generalized audio-visual Saliency prediction

  - training: video, audio, degraded saliency map (ground truth + varying noise)

  - multi-modal interaction mechanism for latent semantic associations
  - simple mean square error loss
  - inference: reversed diffusion, multi-step denoising from random noisy saliency maps
- Properties
  - (i) unlike methods with spatio-temporal visual branching (cite): spatio-temporal modeling of audio and video; audio-only, video-only, audio-visual
  - (ii) iterative denoising -> reuse Saliency-UNet to improve without retraining

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Humans have visual and auditory sensory systems, and with them they can quickly focus on the most interesting areas in their daily activities. This capability of visual attention in multi-modal scenarios has been studied by many researchers and it is called the audio-visual saliency prediction (AVSP) task. Based on the related techniques there are many useful practical applications, from video summarization and compression to virtual reality and augmented reality.

A lot of effort has gone into this area, focusing on improving the quality of multimodal interaction and making the model structures more generalizable. Among the common AVSP approaches, localization-based methods have gotten a lot of attention, as shown in Figure 1 (a). These methods usually treat the sounding objects in the scene as the saliency targets and turn the saliency prediction task into a spatial sound source localization problem. These methods do consider the semantic interactions between audio and visual modalities, but they still do not focus much on a generalized network structure, and this leads to constrained performance.

On the other hand, recent 3D convolution-based methods show better performance in predicting audio-visual saliency maps, as shown in Figure 1 (b). But these methods need customized architectures with built-in inductive biases that are tailored for saliency prediction tasks. For example, Jain et al. and Xiong et al. both use a 3D encoder-decoder structure similar to UNet, but they put their empirical designs into the decoder. Also, both the localization-based and the 3D convolution-based methods use sophisticated loss functions, which makes the audio-visual saliency modeling paradigm more intricate.

Effective audio-visual interaction and a generalized saliency network are two essential factors for applying AVSP technology in the real world. But the existing works have not exploited these two challenges in depth enough. Diffusion models have strong generalization capabilities and can be used as a unified framework for generative tasks with class labels, text prompts, images, and even sounds as the conditions. However, how to design a diffusion model that has both effective audio-visual interaction and a generalized saliency network is still an open question.

In this work we present a conditional Diffusion model for generalized audio-visual Saliency prediction (DiffSal), which tries to address these two challenges at the same time, as shown in Figure 1 (c). DiffSal uses the input video and audio as the conditions and reformulates the prediction problem as a conditional generative task of the saliency map. In training, the model gets the video and audio cues and also a degraded saliency map, which is obtained from the ground-truth by injecting noise with varying degrees. We build a two-stream encoder to explore audio and video feature pairs with spatio-temporal coherence, and the similar pixel-wise multi-modal features we get can be used to guide the generation process of the diffusion model. Also, a novel network Saliency-UNet is used to recover the original saliency maps from the noisy inputs, and it uses information from the spatio-temporal audio and video features as the conditions. We also propose an effective multi-modal interaction mechanism to explore the latent semantic associations between audio and video features. The whole DiffSal framework uses a simple mean square error loss to predict ground-truth saliency maps from random noise. In inference, DiffSal follows the reversed diffusion process and does multi-step denoising to generate predictions from randomly generated noisy saliency maps.

Because of this diffusion-based framework, we show two distinct properties that are appealing for the AVSP task. (i) Existing methods have spatio-temporal visual branching, but DiffSal allows spatio-temporal modeling of audio and video, and it can be generalized to audio-only, video-only, and audio-visual scenarios. (ii) Because the diffusion model has the iterative denoising property, DiffSal can reuse Saliency-UNet iteratively to improve performance without retraining.

To summarize, our main contributions are: (1) We formulate the saliency prediction task as a conditional generative problem and propose a novel conditional diffusion saliency model, which benefits from the generalized network structure and effective audio-visual interaction. (2) We show two properties of DiffSal that are effective for saliency prediction: it can be applied to either uni-modal or multi-modal scenarios, and it can do flexible iterative refinement without retraining. (3) We did extensive experiments on six challenging audio-visual benchmarks, and the results show that DiffSal achieves excellent performance, with an average relative improvement of 6.3% over the previous state-of-the-art results across four metrics.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With their visual and auditory sensory systems, human beings can quickly focus on the most interesting areas during their daily activities. This comprehensive capability of visual attention in multi-modal scenarios has been explored by numerous researchers and is referred to as the audio-visual saliency prediction (AVSP) task. Based on the related techniques, many valuable practical applications have emerged, ranging from video summarization [1] and compression [2] to virtual reality [3] and augmented reality [4].

Significant efforts have been dedicated to this domain, concentrating on improving the quality of multimodal interaction and the generalizability of model structures. Among the prevalent AVSP approaches, as depicted in Figure 1 (a), localization-based methods [5,6,7] have gained a lot of attention. These methods typically consider the sounding objects in the scene as saliency targets and transform the saliency prediction task into a spatial sound source localization problem. Although these methods consider the semantic interactions between audio and visual modalities, their focus on a generalized network structure is still limited, which inevitably results in constrained performance.

In contrast, recent 3D convolution-based methods [8,9,10,11] exhibit superior performance in predicting audio-visual saliency maps, as illustrated in Figure 1 (b). However, these methods require customized architectures with built-in inductive biases tailored for saliency prediction tasks. For instance, Jain et al. [9] and Xiong et al. [11] both adopt a 3D encoder-decoder structure akin to UNet, but integrate their empirical designs into the decoder. Moreover, both localization-based and 3D convolution-based methods employ sophisticated loss functions, leading to a more intricate audio-visual saliency modeling paradigm.

Effective audio-visual interaction and a generalized saliency network are two essential factors for the seamless application of AVSP technology in the real world. Unfortunately, existing works are far from exploiting both challenges in depth. Owing to their strong generalization capabilities, diffusion models [12,13,14] can be employed as a unified framework for generative tasks with class labels [15], text prompts [16], images [17], and even sounds [18] as the modeling conditions. However, how to design a diffusion model that satisfies both effective audio-visual interaction and a generalized saliency network remains an open question.

In this work, we present a conditional Diffusion model for generalized audio-visual Saliency prediction (DiffSal), which aims to tackle these two challenges simultaneously, as illustrated in Figure 1 (c). DiffSal uses the input video and audio as conditions to reformulate the prediction problem as a conditional generative task of the saliency map. During training, the model is fed the video and audio cues together with a degraded saliency map obtained from the ground-truth with varying degrees of injected noise. By constructing a two-stream encoder to explore audio and video feature pairs with spatio-temporal coherence, the resulting similar pixel-wise multi-modal features can be used to guide the generation process of the diffusion model. In addition, a novel network, Saliency-UNet, is employed to recover the original saliency maps from noisy inputs, using information from the spatio-temporal audio and video features as conditions. To explore the latent semantic associations between audio and video features, an effective multi-modal interaction mechanism is proposed. The entire DiffSal framework employs a simple mean square error loss to predict ground-truth saliency maps from random noise. During inference, following the reversed diffusion process, DiffSal performs multi-step denoising to generate predictions from randomly generated noisy saliency maps.

Benefiting from this diffusion-based framework, we demonstrate two distinct properties that appeal to the AVSP task. (i) In contrast to existing methods with spatio-temporal visual branching [6,11,9], DiffSal enables spatio-temporal modeling of audio and video, and can be generalized to audio-only, video-only, and audio-visual scenarios. (ii) Thanks to the iterative denoising property of the diffusion model, DiffSal can iteratively reuse Saliency-UNet to improve performance without retraining.

To summarize, our main contributions are: (1) We formulate the saliency prediction task as a conditional generative problem and propose a novel conditional diffusion saliency model, which benefits from the generalized network structure and effective audio-visual interaction. (2) We demonstrate two properties of DiffSal that are effective for saliency prediction: the ability to be applied to either uni-modal or multi-modal scenarios, and to perform flexible iterative refinement without retraining. (3) Extensive experiments on six challenging audio-visual benchmarks demonstrate that DiffSal achieves excellent performance, with an average relative improvement of 6.3% over the previous state-of-the-art results across four metrics.
